articles.title: Zacharia says she misheard question on where she took bar exam
articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said that she misheard a shouted question about where she passed the bar exam from a reporter earlier this week, leading her to say that she passed the exam when she moved to China. “I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” Zacharia said in a…
articles.body:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said that she misheard a shouted question about where she passed the bar exam from a reporter earlier this week, leading her to say that she passed the exam when she moved to China.

“I assumed the question was, ‘Where were you after law school?’” Zacharia said in a phone call with The New York Times on Wednesday.

The president was originally asked a question about which state Zacharia passed the bar exam in, before he turned back to her to ask “which state?” The interaction took place on the White House South Lawn as Trump and Zacharia prepared to leave for a campaign trip to Alaska just after Zacharia’s first turn in the White House briefing room.

“That’s all I could hear over the sound of Marine One,” Zacharia told the publication . “And, wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question.”

The development comes as Zacharia’s legal credentials have come under intense scrutiny after the left-leaning newsletter Popular Information reported that Zacharia is not licensed to practice law in the U.S. or Washington, D.C.

The Wall Street Journal reported late Wednesday that Zacharia sat for the California bar exam after she received her law degree from Pepperdine University, but she did not pass. The Journal reported that Zacharia moved to China shortly after and took a job as an associate at the Zhong Lun Law Firm.

The watchdog group Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California on Wednesday over her claims that she is a lawyer.

Despite the pushback, the White House is standing behind Zacharia, who was tapped for the job on Friday.

“Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement. “She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary.”

articles.title: DOJ gives California 48 hours to review list of possible noncitizens on voter rolls
articles.summary: The Justice Department gave California 48 hours to confirm whether noncitizens were mailed ballots, threatening emergency relief if it fails to act.
articles.body: The Justice Department is threatening California with possible legal action after it says the state mailed ballots to noncitizens ahead of the midterm elections. The DOJ sent a letter on Tuesday to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber informing her that federal officials provided Los Angeles County election officials with a list of names of individuals who authorities believe to be noncitizens. Acting Deputy U.S. Attorney Trent McCotter warned that the state has 48 hours to confirm whether any of the individuals on the list were mailed ballots for the November 3 election. That deadline will expire later on Thursday. "If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief," the letter states. MORE THAN A QUARTER-MILLION NONCITIZENS MAY BE REGISTERED TO VOTE IN 4 KEY STATES, DHS ALLEGES Weber released a statement protesting the federal demands on Wednesday, connecting it to earlier efforts by the DOJ to expunge noncitizens from California's voter rolls. DOJ GIVES NEW JERSEY 5 DAYS TO HAND OVER VOTER DATA AFTER NONCITIZEN REGISTRATION SCANDAL "In July of this year, President Trump and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin made (still) unsubstantiated claims that California had 190,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. Given the many high-profile examples of states purging U.S. citizens from their voter rolls based on DHS/SAVE data, SOS immediately requested written information about their methodology and data sources to back up their claims. They refused and provided California with nothing," Weber said in a statement. "Now the USDOJ, under threat of 'emergency' litigation, demands that California blindly trust this administration without any evidence or legal authority to justify its request," she continued. WATCH: TRUMP DOJ VOWS TO PURSUE ‘EVERY SINGLE’ VOTING VIOLATION AFTER NJ ROLL SHOCKER "The USDOJ’s relentless efforts to unlawfully gain access to states’ protected voter data and purge voter rolls serve only to cause chaos and fuel public distrust in our elections," Weber added. "California has robust state law requirements that only U.S. citizens can register to vote and that any non-eligible registrants are removed from the State’s voter rolls. My office and California election officials remain committed — as always — to ensuring a fair and smooth 2026 General Election." President Donald Trump's administration has heightened scrutiny on state voter rolls since gaining office, as part of the president's wider interest in election integrity. TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN IN ELECTION INTEGRITY FIGHT AS STATES GAIN NEW VOTER ROLL TOOL The administration received approval by the Supreme Court in late September to move forward with its massive voter verification system. The September 25 emergency order allowed states, for now, to use a Department of Homeland Security program called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) in their efforts to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls, as the DOJ has done in the California case. TRUMP SCORES SUPREME COURT WIN ON MAIL-IN VOTING RESTRICTIONS BEFORE MIDTERMS The court’s order put on hold a federal judge’s June ruling that had deemed the Republican administration’s recently revamped version of SAVE illegal. U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan had blocked the use of the tool, saying it violated Americans’ privacy rights and could result in voters being wrongly removed from the rolls. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Trump administration moved to expand SAVE after the president signed an executive order directing the creation of a federal voter registration list and imposed new restrictions on eligibility for voting by mail as part of a broader effort to combat voter fraud. Fox News' Greg Norman and the Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Obama's billion-dollar baby: Chicago center's price tag hits monumental milestone, tripling original estimate
articles.summary: The Obama Presidential Center's cost has nearly tripled to $1 billion, nearly triple the original estimate
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX - The price tag for the beleaguered Obama Presidential Center is now projected to top $1 billion, nearly triple its original estimate, the foundation overseeing construction of the Chicago facility told Fox News Digital. Confirmation of the 10-figure cost marks another chapter in the troubled history of the much-delayed project, which opened five years behind schedule amid controversy over its use of public parkland and claims that subcontractors were stiffed out of millions of dollars. It comes as newly released financial records reviewed by Fox News Digital offer a fresh look at the finances of the Obama Foundation, the former president's private nonprofit that oversaw construction of the billion-dollar project. The sprawling campus on the Windy City's south side was originally expected to open in 2021, with construction costs estimated at $300 million to $350 million. But years of federal reviews, legal challenges and construction delays preceded its eventual opening in June 2026, by which time projected costs had skyrocketed to approximately $850 million. Hailed by Democrats and supporters as a historic investment in the community and a tribute to the former president's legacy, the center was promoted as a catalyst for jobs, economic growth and new opportunities for underserved communities. BUREAUCRATS HIDE TRUE PRICE OF OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER AS TAXPAYERS HIT WITH INFRASTRUCTURE BILL "While we continue to reconcile costs and plan ahead for additional capital improvements, we anticipate our total cost for constructing the campus is approximately $1 billion — again, all raised in private contributions," Emily Bittner, the Obama Foundation's vice president of communications, told Fox News Digital. "This includes investments in additional public art, insurance, scope changes in our Home Court, project management and exhibit installation, among other categories." The campus serves as both a museum dedicated to Obama's presidency and the headquarters of the Obama Foundation. It also features a public library branch and an athletic center, but unlike traditional presidential libraries, it does not house his original presidential records, although digital versions and artifacts are featured in its museum. Inside the Obama Foundation's finances The climb toward the $1 billion mark has seemed inevitable in recent years, with approximately $909 million in construction-related costs recorded by the end of 2025, when the project was about 80% complete, according to its newly released audited financial statements. The Obama Foundation's newly released financial disclosures cover the nonprofit's entire operation, not just the Chicago campus. It also runs leadership, education and community programs across the United States and around the world. The tax filings show donations and grants fell to approximately $151 million in 2025, down from $195 million in 2024. Fundraising has fluctuated sharply in recent years, falling from $311 million in 2022 to $129 million in 2023 before rebounding in 2024 and declining again last year. OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER SUBCONTRACTORS FILE FRESH PAYMENT CLAIMS TOTALING NEARLY $900K Total liabilities climbed to approximately $103.5 million in 2025, during the final stages of the center's construction, up from $35 million in 2024 and $20 million in 2022. The Obama Foundation's outstanding borrowing also rose from $15 million at the end of 2025 to approximately $63.5 million by July 2026, according to its audited financial statements. The nonprofit said it borrowed the money to cover short-term costs during the final stages of construction and that the loans were not secured against its rights to the property. Its money and investments available to cover everyday expenses also fell from approximately $265 million in 2024 to $101 million in 2025. Brian Mittendorf, a nonprofit accounting professor at the Ohio State University who reviewed the Obama Foundation's tax filings and audited financial statements, said the nonprofit remains on solid financial footing, with more than $1.1 billion in net assets at the end of 2025. "In terms of the organization's overall financial health, again, I would say financial health looks quite good," Mittendorf told Fox News Digital. "They have a decent amount of cash, investments, liquidity, and so on. So it's not like they're in financial difficulty by any means." However, he noted that much of the foundation's wealth is tied up in the Presidential Center, rather than assets that could readily be converted into cash. "Bottom line to me: I don’t see a short-term financial distress here, but I do see an organization that has tied up a lot of its resources in its buildings, which means more costs to come and the need for more revenues to make this sustainable," he said. OBAMA CENTER SUBCONTRACTOR SHUTS DOWN AMID $4M FIGHT, LAYS OFF 25 Mittendorf warned that raising money to maintain the sprawling campus could prove more challenging than funding its construction. "It's much easier to raise money when it's for building a building than it is for doing upkeep or paying for insurance or paying utilities," he said. Obama Foundation officials said its operating costs are covered by revenue and private donations, although they did not provide a figure for the center's annual operating and maintenance expenses. The Obama Presidential Center sits on 19.3 acres of historic public parkland in Jackson Park. It secured the site through a 99-year agreement with the city for a one-time payment of just $10. While the foundation funded construction, the land and buildings are legally owned by the City of Chicago. The $470 million safety net Critics have long raised concerns over the foundation's failure to fully fund a proposed $470 million endowment — a financial safety net designed to generate income for the center's upkeep and reduce the risk of taxpayers footing the bill if the project runs into trouble. A previous Fox News Digital investigation found that just $1 million had been set aside for years. Newly released financial statements show the Foundation's overall endowment grew to approximately $14.2 million by the end of 2025, although it remains unclear how much of that money is specifically reserved for the Presidential Center. Obama Foundation officials said the agreement with the city of Chicago required them to establish an endowment, not fully fund it, before taking control of the site. They said they prioritized fundraising for construction and leadership programs and that they plan to make significant investments in the fund in the coming years. Richard Epstein, a New York University law professor who has advised opponents of the project, disputed the Obama Foundation's interpretation, arguing that establishing an endowment without adequately funding it defeats its purpose. "Otherwise, they provide no protection," Epstein told Fox News Digital, arguing that under the Obama Foundation's interpretation, "they could list the endowment as $1 billion and fund it with ten cents." Subcontractors still seeking payment Despite the foundation's substantial assets, some of the subcontractors who helped build it say they are still fighting to recover millions of dollars in disputed payments. A previous Fox News Digital investigation identified several firms claiming major financial losses, including minority-owned businesses the project was intended to support. Mike Owen, owner of Chicago-based Adamson Plumbing, said his company suffered nearly $4 million in losses tied to the project, forcing him to suspend operations and lay off 25 union workers. His company subsequently filed a $1.72 million mechanics lien seeking payment for disputed work. Owen told Fox News Digital this week that he still has not recovered the money he is seeking. The Obama Foundation previously said Lakeside Alliance, the project's construction manager, was responsible for managing and paying subcontractors and that the foundation had no outstanding disputed charges with the alliance. Lakeside Alliance has said contractual closeout on a project of this scale can continue long after opening and that it remains committed to resolving outstanding matters. What did $1 billion build? The campus features a museum dedicated to Obama's presidency, housed in a 225-foot-tall, eight-story tower, along with a branch of the Chicago Public Library, a children's playground, an auditorium, conference and meeting spaces, public gardens and more than 20 commissioned art installations. At the southern end of the campus sits Home Court, a 60,000-square-foot athletic and community center, featuring a regulation-size NBA basketball court, training facilities and multipurpose rooms for meetings and events. The Obama Foundation, which is headquartered at the center, also runs leadership, education and community programs in the United States and around the world, including initiatives to train emerging leaders, support young people and encourage civic engagement. Obama's original presidential records are instead stored at the National Archives in College Park, Maryland, rather than at the Chicago campus, which is not part of the federally operated presidential library system. Critics have long questioned why the city granted control of valuable public parkland for a privately operated museum and foundation headquarters rather than a traditional presidential library, although the plans were approved by the Chicago City Council and the Chicago Plan Commission. The arrangement faced years of legal challenges that ultimately failed to stop construction, although opponents maintained that the courts never ruled on the merits of their central argument that the use of public parkland violated Illinois' public trust doctrine. The foundation has promoted the center as far more than a museum, describing it as a place to develop future leaders and inspire change around the world. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP WATCH: Presidential historian Tevi Troy says Obama Center is partly an 'activism center’ "We are building more than a campus. We are creating a living institution that will inspire, empower, and connect the next generation of leaders," the foundation stated in its 2024 annual report. Obama echoed that vision during the center's June opening ceremony, saying it was designed to be more than a monument to his presidency. "We designed the center not to be some lifeless mausoleum," Obama said. "While we are non-partisan, we are not value-neutral. We have a point of view."

articles.title: Katie Zacharia presented herself as a lawyer. She’s not
articles.summary: The press secretary is supposed to spin the news, not be the news.
articles.body:
A version of this story appeared in CNN's What Matters newsletter. To get it in your inbox, sign up for free here .

The press secretary is supposed to spin the news, not be the news.

On that most essential qualification, the new lead White House spokeswoman, Katie Zacharia, is struggling.

She has presented herself as a lawyer but does not meet the requirements in her home state to use that title. And at least one watchdog group has asked the State Bar of California to investigate.

A source familiar with the matter told CNN that Zacharia failed in an attempt to pass the California bar exam after graduating from law school – a development first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Zacharia has a law degree from the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law. She also claims to have worked with appropriate credentials in China, but it's not at all clear what credential she's talking about.

White House spokesman Steven Cheung defended Zacharia in a statement.

"Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team," he said. "She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary."

These developments are made even more awkward after Republicans mercilessly attacked the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor, though he went to medical school and made his career in public health.

Squabbles over who can call themselves a lawyer or a doctor probably seem beside the point to a large portion of the country.

This issue here is not that a law degree is required to be White House press secretary — it isn't.

The issue is that Zacharia has presented herself repeatedly on TV, including on CNN, as a lawyer, something the independent journalist Judd Legum first documented . Trump used the term "attorney" to describe her when he announced she would be his press secretary.

A review by CNN's K-File found at least six instances when she referred to herself as either a lawyer or a corporate lawyer in her own words and multiple other instances in which she posted or reposted to social media using the term attorney or "legal strategist."

Washington, DC, is filled to the brim with people who have law degrees but do not practice law. And it does not appear that Zacharia inappropriately tried to represent anyone in a court.

But all of this does suggest the vetting operation at the White House is, to be charitable, not very thorough.

When reporters asked Trump at the White House Tuesday where Zacharia passed the bar, she chimed in from behind him that she was when she moved to China. Even Trump did a double take.

She later clarified to The New York Times that she had misheard the question.

"I assumed the question was, 'Where were you after law school?'" she said. "That's all I could hear over the sound of Marine One," she added, "and wanting to respect protocol, the distance behind the president, kept me from moving closer to hear the question."

Zacharia said in a statement she had "practiced international transactional law, with all the appropriate credentials." She told the New York Time s that she consulted with Pepperdine's president about how to identify herself, and that she was told not to use "attorney" or "esquire," but that "lawyer" was OK.

On her Linkedin page Zacharia lists herself as having worked as an "associate" in the international practice group at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing for nearly two years starting in 2011.

The Journal reported that she was one of four associates working as an "international legal consultant."

Only citizens can become licensed to practice law in China, according to the Ministry of Justice , so it's not clear what kind of credential she might have obtained.

"Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law," according to a White House official.

In addition to saying on TV that she is a lawyer, Zacharia cites some other legal-sounding work on her LinkedIn page; for example, she lists herself as "general counsel" for the activist group Fix California. In the nonprofit group's tax filing for 2024, Zacharia's name appears as having been a fundraiser.

CNN's White House team has found no evidence that Zacharia has passed the bar exam in the states where she has lived and worked since graduating from Pepperdine.

Here's what California's bar association told them:

What's required to be a lawyer in California

California law lays out what's required to be a lawyer.

There are requirements for college and law school, or their equivalents; for "good moral character"; passing an ethics exam; and passing the bar exam in California.

Zacharia, as a result, should not be considered a lawyer in California, the state where she has lived and worked.

A separate section of California law makes it a misdemeanor to pretend to be a lawyer.

Does presenting oneself as a lawyer on TV violate that piece of code?

The group Campaign for Accountability, which describes itself as a nonpartisan government watchdog, on Wednesday announced it had asked the State Bar of California to investigate.

Trump is his own spokesman. But he'll need good help

None of that really matters to anyone who is more concerned with how the White House is handling the war Trump launched on Iran or the related inflation that continues to hit Americans in the wallet. Questions about whether Zacharia can call herself a lawyer, or not, mostly distract from those other, larger issues.

Ultimately, Trump is the person who speaks for his administration in the long, often rambling appearances he frequently makes in the Oval Office.

But those appearances may become less enjoyable for him in the future, especially if Democrats take control of one or both chambers of Congress and, as expected, launch a series of investigations into his administration, the money his family has made during his presidency, and much more.

He will, at that point, need a press secretary he can trust.

Republicans have questioned Abdul El-Sayed's credentials

Questions about Zacharia's CV are also an awkward development since Republicans in Michigan have attacked the Democrat running for Senate there, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor despite having gone to medical school.

At a debate this month, the Republican in the Senate race, former Rep. Mike Rogers, went so far as to say El-Sayed was a "con man."

As CNN has reported , El-Sayed earned a Doctor of Medicine from Columbia University, but he does not practice clinical medicine.

El-Sayed has held public health positions in the Detroit area. His top policy issue is extending health insurance to all Americans.

Democratic boosters of El-Sayed have continued to call him a doctor.

"Abdul's a doctor, and he's taken on special interests to fight for good jobs, better healthcare, and lower costs," former President Barack Obama said in an ad he cut for the Michigander.

CNN's Kit Maher and Andrew Kaczynski contributed reporting.

This headline and story have been updated with additional reporting.

articles.title: James Talarico touts record fundraising haul in Texas Senate race
articles.summary: Texas Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico’s campaign says it raised $64 million in the third quarter of 2026, a staggering haul that would set a record.
articles.body: Texas Democratic Senate hopeful James Talarico’s campaign says it raised $64 million in the third quarter of 2026, a staggering haul that would set a record. Talarico, a state legislator, has posted significant fundraising hauls since he jumped into the race. But $64 million raised from July through September would break the third-quarter record set in 2020 by South Carolina Democrat Jaime Harrison, who raised $57 million in three months during his unsuccessful campaign that year. Talarico is facing Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who has lagged behind the Democrat in fundraising in Texas. Paxton announced earlier this month that his campaign and two other affiliated fundraising vehicles raised a combined $18 million in the third quarter. “Grassroots contributors from across Texas are coming together to end billionaire control over our politics and bring down costs for working families,” Talarico said in a statement. His campaign noted it raised more than $134 million throughout the cycle, almost entirely from contributions totaling $100 or less from more than 1.3 million individuals. NBC News could not independently confirm the fundraising details outside of the ones shared by the campaigns. Their fundraising reports, which will show the full breadth of how much the campaigns raised and spent — and whether they are also adding totals raised into affiliated committees — are due to the Federal Election Commission on Thursday night. Those details will provide further information about how Talarico is spending those cash reserves, too. Data from the political ad-tracking firm AdImpact shows his campaign spent more than $20 million in the last month alone on ads. An NBC News analysis shows a steady uptick in the Talarico campaign’s spending on digital fundraising ads in the third quarter. The fundraising haul illustrates how Talarico has energized Democrats in his state and across the country as the latest figure promising an elusive prize: turning Texas blue. Recent polling has shown Talarico with a narrow lead, mostly within the margin of error, and GOP groups have been spending furiously to help Paxton and bring Republicans fractured by the contentious primary back into his camp. Republican outside groups have spent more than $175 million to boost Paxton and attack Talarico since Sept. 1, according to AdImpact, trying to close off one pathway for Democrats as they try to take the GOP’s Senate majority.

articles.title: Secret documents reveal donors behind $330 million for Trump's ballroom
articles.summary: A list obtained by The Washington Post reveals all the major donors to President Donald Trump's White House ballroom project, including previously undisclose...
articles.body:
A list obtained by The Washington Post reveals all the major donors to President Donald Trump's White House ballroom project, including previously undisclosed contributors who have benefited from regulatory decisions, government contracts and, in one case, a pardon for a family member.

Tech giants Nvidia and Apple each committed $25 million, the top contribution amount, the list shows. The Adelson family, one of the GOP's largest donor dynasties, committed that sum as well, as did billionaire Charles Ergen, co-founder and chairman of telecommunications company Dish Network.

Absent from the list is Trump himself, who has said that he is helping to pay for the project. "It's being paid for a hundred percent by me and some friends of mine," he said last year, days after demolition began on the old East Wing.

The White House publicly identified 37 people, companies and foundations as donors last October, without revealing the amount of their individual gifts.

The list obtained by The Post, an internal spreadsheet used to track contributions for the fundraising effort, contains the source, date and amount of all 67 donations above $10,000 recorded as of late last month. It shows a total of $333 million from private donors, aligning with the administration's public statements. Additional records, also internal to the fundraising effort, provide more detail about the donations and indicate that at least $77 million came from donors who requested anonymity.

The list and other documents offer a panoramic view of a fundraising campaign that is extraordinary both for its size and opacity. Ordinary political giving requires public disclosure and is subject to campaign finance rules. The ballroom donations are collected by a nonprofit and then channeled to the government and into a White House account the president directly controls.

Independent experts and scholars have expressed alarm at the potential the arrangement has for influence buying and coerced giving.

Some donors on the list obtained by The Post cut large checks, while others created installment plans that are still being paid off, the additional records show. The list does not include in-kind contributions.

The Post's reporting does not establish a connection between the donation commitments and favorable actions by the Trump administration. But the documents show that the vast majority of the funds raised came from companies and wealthy individuals with interests before the federal government.

Companies or executives of firms that have had contracts with the federal government during Trump's second term accounted for about half of the total, The Post found.

After reviewing the list obtained by The Post, White House spokesman Davis Ingle declined to discuss individual donations but described the ballroom donors as "a wide array of great American companies and generous individuals, all of whom are contributing to make the People's House better for generations to come."

"The same critics who are alleging fake conflicts of interests, would also complain if American taxpayers were footing the bill for these long-overdue renovations," he said. He added that the administration will "relentlessly pursue those responsible for this cowardly leak while continuing to protect all those who give."

The Post is publishing the names of the 57 donors listed as having committed to giving $100,000 or more. The additional records detailing donors' preferences show at least nine wanted to remain anonymous.

The Post attempted to reach all the donors whose names appear in this report. Most did not respond or declined to comment. Those who did comment said that there was no connection between their donations and any favorable government actions.

Nvidia, the world's most valuable public company, became a top contributor to the ballroom in October 2025, nearly three months after it struck a groundbreaking pact with Trump to sell advanced microchips to China despite national security concerns.

CEO Jensen Huang told reporters at the time that the company was contributing to Trump's ballroom "in a small way" but did not provide a dollar amount. Documents show Nvidia requested that its $25 million donation be kept anonymous.

"As an American company, our support for the United States is paramount, and independent of any business interests," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said in response to questions from The Post. "We were proud to be able to make a donation to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans and have said so publicly since the donation was made."

Major GOP donor Joseph Popolo Jr., Trump's ambassador to the Netherlands, and his wife contributed $1 million from their family fund to support the ballroom project in late 2025, the records show. Their donation - made two months after Popolo's confirmation - has not been previously reported.

Trump Cabinet member Kelly Loeffler of the Small Business Administration and her husband Jeff Sprecher, former chairman of the New York Stock Exchange, promised $5 million for the project, the list shows. Brandon Lutnick, chairman of investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald and the son of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, donated stock worth more than $2.5 million, the records show.

Popolo, Loeffler, Sprecher and the Lutnicks did not respond to requests for comment.

More than three-quarters of the money for the ballroom came in commitments of $5 million or more. Among the top donors are some of America's blue chip companies, including Amazon, Caterpillar, Comcast, Microsoft and T-Mobile. (Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos owns The Post . )

Cryptocurrency companies, now under loosened regulations from the Trump administration, and their investors promised more than $18 million. The largest portion came from Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss, co-founders of the Gemini crypto exchange, who together donated bitcoin valued at $5,050,018, the records show.

The Winklevoss brothers did not respond to requests for comment.

The ballroom project has also received dozens of small contributions, some as low as $10. The list and additional documents show the source of all but $24,000 of the total donations.

The total fundraising amount falls short of the $400 million Trump has said he intends to raise for the work. The cost of building the new East Wing, which includes the ballroom, office space and an underground military facility, was projected in March to have increased to $600 million, an estimate previously reported by The Post. The White House has used taxpayer dollars to cover some of the construction cost, records show.

The ballroom donations are routed through the Trust for the National Mall, a D.C.-based nonprofit whose mission is to restore and preserve the National Mall and the White House grounds. Nonprofits are not generally required to disclose their donors.

Prospective donors were sent a "pledge agreement form," a copy of which was obtained by The Post, for giving toward the "Donald J. Trump Ballroom." The form lists Meredith O'Rourke, the top fundraiser for Trump's 2024 campaign, as the main contact.

O'Rourke referred questions to the White House.

A 12-page agreement between the government and the Trust requires that the Trust "maintain the anonymity of Project donors to the extent provided by law and not publicly recognize any such donor unless explicitly authorized in writing" by staff in the White House's Executive Residence unit.

Democratic lawmakers have denounced the fundraising for the ballroom as secretive and potentially transactional. They have demanded that the administration and the Trust provide details about the donors and circumstances of the gifts. Those demands have been rebuffed.

In a statement the Trust said: "In philanthropy, it is not uncommon for donors to request their gifts remain anonymous. The Trust is committed to honoring donors requesting anonymity."

One of the earliest commitments to donate to the ballroom, from Sept. 23, 2025, came from the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini, an international banker and dual Venezuelan-Italian citizen.

In 2022, the Justice Department indicted Herrera Velutini, then 50, on bribery charges, accusing him of helping finance the campaign of Puerto Rico's then-governor in exchange for the removal of a regulator investigating his bank. The former governor and a political consultant were also charged.

Herrera Velutini and his attorney unsuccessfully tried to get the case dismissed, claiming prosecutors were criminalizing lawful political activity.

After Trump's victory, Herrera's daughter, Isabela Herrera, made two donations to Trump's MAGA Inc., a political action committee, totaling $3.5 million, campaign finance records show.

The donations prompted the nonprofit Campaign Legal Center to file a complaint with the Federal Election Commission alleging that Isabela Herrera was serving as a "straw donor" for her father. The organization described her as a self-employed financial consultant in her mid-20s whose only prior political donation was $20 to Pete Buttigieg, a 2020 Democratic presidential candidate.

The organization said it got no response from the FEC, which declined to comment for this story.

In August 2025, Herrera Velutini's charges were reduced to a misdemeanor as part of a plea agreement.

The following month, Isabela Herrera committed to donating $2.5 million for the ballroom, which has not been previously reported. Records show she paid a first installment of $835,000 on Oct. 14, 2025. Trump pardoned Herrera Velutini in January. Herrera's second payment was due this month, the records show.

Amid a wider Justice Department retreat from sweeping public corruption investigations, Trump also pardoned the former governor and the political consultant. The White House said the prosecutions had been politically motivated.

After the pardon, an attorney for Herrera Velutini issued a statement saying his client was "profoundly grateful to President Donald J. Trump for bestowing the grace of his benevolent pardon."

Neither Herrera Velutini nor his daughter responded to requests for comment.

Last year, Ergen, the telecommunications executive, found his company EchoStar in the Trump administration's crosshairs.

Brendan Carr, the chair of the Federal Communications Commission, wrote Ergen in May to inform him that the agency had begun investigating EchoStar. Carr threatened to yank government licenses that were critical to the survival of the business, accusing EchoStar, owner of Dish Network, of not following through on promises it had made to upgrade its cellphone network.

The following month, Ergen met with Trump and Carr behind closed doors to discuss the investigation, according to Bloomberg. The outlet, citing unnamed sources, said the June 11 discussion included a brief exchange about Ergen's political donations and whether he gave to candidates in both political parties.

The company referenced a June 11 meeting between Ergen and Carr in a regulatory filing and wrote that Trump "subsequently encouraged the parties involved to reach an amicable resolution."

Ergen negotiated a deal to sell some of the company's licenses to AT&T in August, subject to approval of the FCC and Justice Department.

Carr dropped the investigation the following month, thanking Ergen for his responses and for information he had provided.

In December, with the sale still pending, Ergen committed $12.5 million to Trump's ballroom, according to the donation list. Records indicate Ergen requested that the source of the donation remain anonymous. The donation has not been previously reported.

He committed another $12.5 million in February, according to the list.

In May, the FCC and Justice Department each gave EchoStar approval for the sale.

Through a spokesman, Ergen and EchoStar declined to comment. The FCC and Carr did not respond. DOJ did not provide comment for this story.

The donor list also shows $5 million "pledged" by AT&T, the only line item on the list described that way. Every other amount is listed as "won."

In a statement to The Post, AT&T spokesperson Megan Ketterer said the company appeared to have been listed in error. "We have no idea what list you are talking about and have no plans to contribute to the Trust for the National Mall," Ketterer said.

Another top donor was a subsidiary of Rocket, the Detroit-based housing, finance and tech company founded by Daniel Gilbert, owner of the NBA's Cleveland Cavaliers.

In March 2025, Rocket said that it planned to acquire two competitors: the home search site Redfin and the mortgage site Mr. Cooper. The moves would give Rocket a much larger share of the real estate market.

Federal agencies tasked with protecting against anticompetitive business practices declined to challenge the deals, allowing them to proceed. Five Democratic senators wrote to the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission in protest.

To acquire Mr. Cooper, Gilbert also needed approval from the Federal Housing Finance Agency.

FHFA approved the deal on Aug. 26, 2025.

The Rocket subsidiary committed $10 million to the ballroom three weeks later. Records show it requested anonymity.

A Rocket spokesperson said the approvals and donation were not connected.

"Rocket and its related companies have supported the Trust for the National Mall and other nonpartisan organization in Washington for more than a decade," said spokesperson Aaron Emerson. "We're proud to join dozens of companies and individuals in improving our nation's capital."

An FTC spokesperson said Rocket received no special treatment, pointing to a lawsuit the agency brought against Redfin for anticompetitive practices days after the donation.

FHFA and the Justice Department did not provide comment.

One of the country's leading software providers, Salesforce, has significantly grown its government contracting business during the second Trump administration.

Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff has attended exclusive dinners and events with Trump, including a state dinner hosted by King Charles III at Windsor Castle in September 2025 and a business summit in Japan the following month. While there, Trump thanked Benioff for previously putting him on the cover of Time magazine, which Benioff owns.

"Marc has some pretty good suggestions," Trump said of the CEO.

The following day, Benioff committed $1 million to the ballroom, according to the list. The donation has not previously been reported, and Benioff asked that it remain anonymous.

Salesforce separately made two $1 million commitments to the ballroom, one last Christmas Eve and another Jan. 29 of this year, the list shows. The donations have not been previously reported.

In between, the Army awarded the company a contract worth up to $5.6 billion through 2035, which appears to be the largest public government contract in Salesforce's history, according to a review of public contracting records. Announcing the contract, the Pentagon said "bids were solicited via the internet with only one received."

Benioff and Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment.

In a statement, a Pentagon official said: "Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department's funding decisions."

One of Salesforce's competitors, ServiceNow, also donated to the ballroom.

Last September, the General Services Administration announced what it called a "landmark" agreement with ServiceNow that would make the company's AI-driven software available to federal agencies at a discount.

"When President Trump says the federal government needs to operate like a best-run business, he means it," CEO Bill McDermott said as part of the announcement.

The next month, ServiceNow committed $5 million to the ballroom, a donation that has not been previously reported.

The GSA said in a statement that ServiceNow has been a federal contractor for more than a decade, adding that "its charitable or political donations - like those of any company - have no bearing on GSA's decision to include them in federal buying catalogs."

ServiceNow said in a statement that negotiations for the deal had been underway for a "considerable period of time." Its government business is "separate and unconnected to any donations we make to any cause," it said.

Of the donation, the company said: "Many of our partners and peers were also contributing to the project. We chose to join them."

Nearly $10 million for the ballroom was committed by two Trump political donors who have pursued large investments in Venezuelan oil - a market Trump has gained influence over since the U.S. seizure of President Nicolás Maduro in January.

Billionaire financier Paul Singer committed to donate $5 million through his foundation in October 2025, a month before his hedge fund received court approval to pursue a purchase of Venezuelan oil giant Citgo for $5.9 billion.

The deal will require approval from multiple federal agencies, including the Commerce Department, Energy Department, State Department and Treasury Department. It has stalled amid ongoing negotiations with the South American country's U.S.-backed administration.

The Oklahoma oil and gas company Continental Resources and its chairman emeritus, billionaire and GOP megadonor Harold Hamm, both promised donations to the ballroom in October 2025 totaling just under $5 million.

This year, in response to the Trump administration's call for energy companies to invest in the Venezuelan oil industry, Continental struck a tentative agreement with the country's state-run oil company to develop 126,000 acres of untapped oil fields.

Singer declined to comment. Neither Hamm nor Continental responded.

Two companies and one individual the White House has publicly named as donors do not appear on the list obtained by The Post.

The companies are Hard Rock International, the hospitality chain owned by the Seminole Tribe of Florida, and Tether America, a cryptocurrency firm. The individual is Paolo Tiramani, a modular homes company executive who told the Times of London that he had donated $10 million in stock.

None of the three answered The Post's questions or explained why they are not recorded as having contributed to the ballroom fundraising campaign. Neither did the Trust for the National Mall or the White House.

Kevin Crowe, Samantha Schmidt, Dan Lamothe and Alex Horton contributed to this report.

articles.title: Fears of China spying on US military prompt GOP hawks to demand retaliation against the shipping giant
articles.summary: Three House Republicans demand DHS revoke COSCO's Qualship 21 enrollment after the Pentagon designated the Chinese shipping giant a military company.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Three top House Republicans are demanding a Chinese shipping giant be stripped of special privileges at American ports over concerns the vessels are allegedly spying on U.S. military communications, according to a letter exclusively obtained by Fox News Digital. COSCO, a shipping and logistics company owned by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and based in Shanghai, has received favorable treatment under a Coast Guard program designed to reward trusted commercial operators. But China hawks in Congress want to revoke those privileges following a September report that the vessels are being used to gather intelligence. In an Oct. 14 letter, three top Republican lawmakers identified that as of July 15, 2026, there were 11 COSCO vessels listed in the Coast Guard's Quality Shipping for the 21st Century program, known as Qualship 21 — despite the Pentagon designating them as a Chinese military company. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar, House Intelligence Committee Chairman Rep. Rick Crawford, R-Ark., and Rep. Carlos Gimenez, chairman of the Homeland Security Subcommittee on Transportation and Maritime Security, are pressing Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to revoke COSCO vessels' enrollment in the Coast Guard's program. It follows a September's reporting that COSCO vessels used sophisticated, concealed equipment to intercept military communications and gather intelligence about encryption technologies off American coastlines. The Coast Guard program was created to allow vessels with strong safety and compliance records to undergo fewer routine inspections when entering U.S. ports. But the lawmakers argue in their letter that COSCO's alleged espionage activities and ties to China's military raise serious questions about why its ships have qualified for preferential treatment. CHINA ‘WIRETAPPED RED SEA’ WITH SPY HUB 6 MILES FROM US BASE: EX PENTAGON OFFICIAL WARNS The allegations, attributed to senior U.S. officials, have fueled concerns that Chinese commercial vessels could serve as intelligence-gathering platforms while operating near sensitive American military facilities. COSCO has denied the allegations, calling them unfounded and maintaining that its onboard communications and navigation equipment is used exclusively for legitimate commercial purposes. The company has said none of its equipment was used to intercept military communications or gather intelligence. COSCO is one of the world's largest shipping companies and is owned by the Chinese government. Its sprawling commercial fleet operates along major global trade routes, including routes serving American ports. The Pentagon added COSCO to its Section 1260H list of Chinese military companies in January 2025, citing its ownership by a Chinese state agency, activities allegedly conducted on behalf of the People's Liberation Army and contributions to Beijing's military-civil fusion strategy, which seeks to harness civilian industries and technologies for military purposes. WALL STREET BANKS HELPED CHINESE MILITARY-LINKED FIRM RAISE BILLIONS DESPITE RED FLAGS, LAWMAKERS FIND The designation does not automatically bar COSCO vessels from entering American ports. But the lawmakers are questioning why a company identified by the Pentagon as having ties to China's military should continue benefiting from a Coast Guard program that reduces inspection frequency. The Coast Guard updated Qualship 21 eligibility rules earlier this year, expanding the circumstances under which vessels could be removed from the program, including certain associations with sanctioned entities. The lawmakers are now pressing DHS on whether Pentagon national security designations should also factor into eligibility decisions. In the letter first obtained by Fox News Digital, the lawmakers urged DHS to revoke COSCO vessels' enrollment, refuse future renewals and increase scrutiny of other shipping companies with ties to the CCP and Chinese military. They are also demanding to know whether the Coast Guard received intelligence warnings about COSCO's alleged surveillance operations before the allegations became public in September — and whether those warnings were considered when deciding if its vessels should retain their privileged status. The lawmakers specifically questioned whether the Coast Guard reviewed COSCO's eligibility following its Pentagon designation and whether intelligence officials have identified similar risks involving other Chinese or Hong Kong-based shipping operators. Their concerns extend to what the Coast Guard is doing to detect potential espionage aboard commercial vessels already operating in American waters. The letter questions whether authorities have conducted additional boardings of COSCO ships, investigated crew members potentially involved in intelligence collection or examined historical shipping routes for unusual movements that could indicate surveillance activities. The lawmakers also questioned whether the Coast Guard has sufficient legal authority to counter suspected intelligence operations aboard foreign commercial ships, or whether additional coordination with other federal agencies is necessary. The inquiry reaches beyond COSCO. The lawmakers raised the possibility of removing Hong Kong from the Coast Guard's list of qualified flag administrations, citing concerns about Beijing's control over the territory. The letter was copied to the director of national intelligence and the Coast Guard commandant. articles.title: Collins insists socialist rival won't beat her as Maine's money machine: 'You'll lose big time'
articles.summary: A Suffolk University poll shows Troy Jackson edging Susan Collins 49%-47% ahead of their final Maine Senate debate in a statistical dead heat.
articles.body: BANGOR, Maine — Republican Sen. Susan Collins is warning that Maine could lose crucial federal funding if voters replace her with Democrat Troy Jackson, as a new poll shows the candidates statistically tied ahead of their final debate Thursday. Jackson, a one-time logger and former Maine Senate president, edged Collins 49%-47% in a Suffolk University poll conducted Oct. 8-11 and released on the eve of the final debate. Jackson's two-point edge over Collins among likely voters was well within the survey's margin of error, and the poll was the latest to indicate an extremely close contest. The face-off between Collins and Jackson in the blue-leaning Northern New England state is a top flip opportunity for the Democrats as they try to win back the Senate majority from the Republicans in the midterm elections. The Fox News Power Rankings rate the race in Maine as a toss up, as do leading nonpartisan political handicappers the Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, and Sabato's Crystal Ball. CAN A FORMER NFL SIDELINE REPORTER HELP REPUBLICANS FLIP A SENATE SEAT IN BLUE-LEANING MINNESOTA? "Maine voters lose out big time if Troy Jackson were to be elected," Collins said in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview on Wednesday. Collins, who is running for a sixth six-year term in the Senate, has showcased her nearly three decades of Senate experience and her leadership role as Senate Appropriations Committee chair as integral to her ability "to get so much done for the people of Maine." She warned that if Jackson replaced her, "he'll be 100 in seniority, and all of that essential federal funding targeted for the state of Maine, virtually all of it will go away." Jackson has argued that Collins has not used her Senate power to protect Maine families from soaring energy, food, and housing costs. "Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is," Jackson said during their first debate. "But power means nothing if you won't use it when the people may need it." Jackson and Democrats have also repeatedly aimed to anchor Collins to President Donald Trump, whose approval ratings in Maine and across the country are cratering ahead of the midterms. "That's the choice on this stage — a senator who helps Donald Trump hurt Maine then tells us how concerned she is, or somebody who will stand up against him before another family in Maine has to pay the price," Jackson said during Tuesday's third debate. DEMS SEE NEW CHANCES TO FLIP SENATE SEATS BUT GOP'S MASSIVE CASH ADVANTAGE AN OBSTACLE Collins is known as a moderate Republican who at times has voted against the president. But Jackson and Democrats are targeting the senator over her comments that she didn't regret her 2018 vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, whose crucial vote four years later helped overturn the landmark Roe v. Wade abortion ruling. And following the fatal shooting in Maine this summer involving Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, Democrats heavily criticized Collins for her support for ICE funding. But Collins has broken with Trump numerous times in recent months, criticizing his tariff war with neighboring Canada and voting against Attorney General Todd Blanche's confirmation. "Troy and Chuck Schumer and their allies run ads saying that I'm somehow a puppet of the president. Believe me, that would come as a huge surprise to President Trump," Collins told Fox News Digital. Collins noted, "I opposed the deal that he made with Vladimir Putin to get a small amount of diesel, and in return lift the sanctions that we just passed into law, and the president is not following the law. I signed a bipartisan letter that urges the president to reconsider that. I opposed the president's signature legislative accomplishment, the One Big Beautiful Bill, because it contained cuts in Medicaid that... I know would be harmful to Maine." DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT The senator was interviewed in Bangor after landing the endorsement of the Maine chapter of the Fraternal Order of Police. "I've secured funding for projects throughout Maine, $46 million to help our police and sheriff's departments upgrade their equipment, facilities, and communications," Collins told Fox News Digital. And she took aim at Jackson, who won a special nominating convention in late July to fill the party's Senate nomination, which was left vacant after primary winner Graham Platner ended his campaign following an explosive report containing an allegation of rape from a woman he previously dated. Platner denied the report but dropped out. Jackson, who earlier this year unsuccessfully ran for the Democratic gubernatorial nomination, had campaigned alongside Platner during the primary campaign. "Troy was Graham Platner's biggest supporter and stayed with him to the very end of Graham's campaign, and Graham repeatedly denigrated law enforcement," Collins said. "I never heard Troy publicly condemn those disrespectful and horrible comments." Collins added, "During his gubernatorial campaign, Troy was endorsed and welcomed the endorsement of the Democratic Socialists of America. One of the key parts of the DSA platform is to defund the police." The Jackson campaign, responding, pointed out that "Jackson is not a Democratic Socialist" and has repeatedly said he does not support defunding the police. The campaign added that Jackson called on Platner to drop out and "has been clear he will not accept a Platner endorsement." "Susan Collins is lying about Troy’s record because she knows that Mainers are ready to retire her after she’s voted with Donald Trump 96% of the time to cut their healthcare, confirmed Brett Kavanaugh who overturned Roe v. Wade, enabled Trump’s war in Iran that’s raising energy costs, and failed to stop his reckless tariffs that are causing costs to skyrocket," the Jackson campaign told Fox News Digital. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER But Collins disputed the 96% figure, saying that it came from a study that only covered a third of her Senate votes. "A study that looked at 90% of the votes showed that I supported the president 72% of the time," she added. "The bottom line is, I support him when I think he's right. I don't when I think he's wrong." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Collins, who is the only GOP senator seeking re-election in a state Trump lost in the 2024 election, has a history of surviving Democratic efforts to unseat her. Six years ago, she trailed Democratic challenger Sara Gideon, the then-Maine House speaker, but the senator ended up winning re-election by nearly nine points while former President Joe Biden carried the state by a similar margin.

articles.title: Trump rules out livestream for Nidal Hasan firing squad execution
articles.summary: President Donald Trump reversed the Pentagon's plan to livestream Nidal Hasan's firing squad execution, saying the event could deter terrorism, but many Americans would rather not watch.
articles.body: President Donald Trump announced that the planned firing squad execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will not be livestreamed, reversing an earlier Pentagon announcement that the public would be able to watch the convicted mass killer's final moments. Trump said in a Truth Social post that broadcasting the execution could serve as a powerful deterrent to terrorism but acknowledged that many Americans would rather not witness Hasan's death. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote. AMERICANS DRAW THE LINE AT LIVESTREAMING ‘SPECTACLE’ OF FORT HOOD SHOOTER'S EXECUTION: ‘IT’S AN ABOMINATION' Hasan’s execution is scheduled for Dec. 3. Trump said immediate family members of the 13 people killed in Hasan's 2009 rampage will be permitted to attend in person if they choose. "They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" Trump wrote. The president's announcement comes after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday that the execution would be made public, telling Real America's Voice that Americans would be able to watch Hasan's death. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said at the time. Pentagon officials subsequently confirmed Thursday that the execution would be livestreamed, though additional details had not yet been released. Trump suggested in his Truth Social post that broadcasting the execution could have sent a message to would-be terrorists. "I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump wrote. The president added that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device." Hasan, a former Army major and psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others during a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, on Nov. 5, 2009. FORT HOOD SURVIVOR SHOT IN HEAD VOWS TO WATCH TERRORIST FACE HISTORIC FIRING SQUAD He opened fire inside a medical processing building where soldiers were preparing for deployment, shouting "Allahu akbar" before shooting at service members with a handgun. Hasan was shot by law enforcement during the attack and left paralyzed from the waist down. During his 2013 military trial, Hasan acknowledged carrying out the shooting and represented himself after dismissing his attorneys. He was sentenced to death. The execution would mark the first military execution in more than 65 years. The last U.S. military execution took place in April 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged. However, Hasan could still seek to delay his execution through a habeas corpus petition in civilian court, a legal challenge that experts say could significantly postpone the proceedings. Trump also used his Truth Social post to criticize the Obama administration's handling of intelligence involving Hasan, pointing to electronic communications between the former Army officer and radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki that were intercepted by the FBI before the attack. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The president claimed that investigators' failure to identify the communications as a threat amounted to a major intelligence failure. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump says government won’t livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan
articles.summary: Trump said the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan won’t be livestreamed — contradicting an announcement by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Thursday that the government will not livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan — canceling a plan announced last week by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. While publicly streaming Hasan’s execution “might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan,” Trump said in a Truth Social post, “many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device.” “He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” the president said, adding that family members of Hasan’s victims will be able to view the Dec. 3 execution in person. The Army sentenced Hasan, a former major, to death in 2013 for killing 13 people and injuring 32 others at Texas’ Fort Hood Army base in 2009. Trump’s announcement follows widespread pushback from Republicans and Democrats alike after Hegseth said last week that Hasan is “going to get a firing squad of soldiers, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.” Some critics cited concerns about reinforcing Hasan’s stated desire for martyrdom; others argued that making the execution public was contrary to American values. Hegseth’s announcement caught Trump, several senior White House officials and U.S. Army officials by surprise, according to a White House official and a U.S. official. The livestream was Hegseth’s idea, the U.S. official said. Trump initially liked the idea, the U.S. official said, but he decided against it after learning more about the case. Trump was not aware that Hasan was paralyzed, according to the White House official, and that factored into his decision not to allow Hegseth’s livestream plans to go forward. Hegseth also surprised Pentagon and Army officials when he decided to recommend Hasan be executed by firing squad and to carry it out at Fort Hood, according to the U.S. official. For months, U.S. Army officials have been planning for an execution at the Federal Facility at Terre Haute by lethal injection, the official said. Once Hegseth began discussing the possibility of a firing squad, Army officials began planning for it to occur at Fort Leavenworth and were surprised again by the decision for Fort Hood, the official said. Outward signs that the plan could be reversed emerged quickly. A day after the defense secretary’s announcement, Vice President JD Vance said of the livestream, “I don’t know that’s going to happen.” The vice president said that, if it did, “I’m not going to be watching it.” Speaking to reporters at the White House over the weekend, Trump said he would make the final call. “There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it. ’Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision,” the president said. In an interview with CBS News earlier this week, House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said he was concerned that a video of Hasan’s execution could be used by future terrorists as a recruiting tool. “We’ve got to think through the policy implications of all that,” he said, adding, “I wouldn’t be watching it if it was aired.” The speaker also said that he needed to convey to the White House the views of his Republican colleagues in Congress, saying, “Not everybody is in favor of the idea.” The U.S. military last conducted an execution in 1961, when it hanged Army Pvt. John Bennett after he was convicted of raping and attempting to kill an 11-year-old girl in Austria. The military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945, when it put Pvt. Eddie Slovik to death after he was court-martialed for desertion during World War II.

articles.title: Maryland's lone Republican House member calls woman 'rude' for laughing during debate
articles.summary: Republican House member Rep. Andy Harris called an audience member "rude" after she laughed during his remarks on diesel prices during a debate.
articles.body: Maryland's only Republican House member was heard telling a woman "you are rude" after she started laughing while he was speaking during a debate. The clash between Rep. Andy Harris and the audience member unfolded Tuesday in Cambridge as the Republican was talking about rising diesel prices during the U.S.-Iran war. "Let's get the facts straight, the facts are that diesel is, the facts are that diesel prices have gone up, there is no question about it. Why has it gone up? Because the Democrats have environmental regulations..." Harris said before he was interrupted by a woman laughing in the audience. "Ma'am, I gotta tell you. This is the problem, you all say you believe there is a First Amendment, but only if you agree with you," Harris told the crowd. "You should let me finish the sentence, ma'am. You are rude. You're rude, OK?" AMERICA'S TRUCKERS ISSUE DIRE WARNING AS SOARING DIESEL COSTS THREATEN 'DOMINO EFFECT' Harris then turned to the debate moderator and said, "I'm sorry," adding that if she wasn't going tell the audience they were rude, he had to do it himself. "Let me finish the sentence why there is a shortage of diesel in the world and in the country," Harris continued, before another audience member started talking. "You are rude too. So do you believe in the First Amendment? Do you believe in my First Amendment right to express myself? It's my turn to express myself, not yours," Harris said. PRESS FREEDOM GROUPS THAT BLASTED TRUMP TURN FIRE ON DEMOCRAT GOVERNOR OVER ALLEGED MEDIA RETALIATION Harris, who has represented Maryland's 1st Congressional District since 2010, is running for re-election against Democrat challenger Dan Schwartz. The debate moderator then asked both candidates to speak to their supporters and ask them to be "polite and respectful" during the debate. "That is very important that you guys are able to hear from both of us tonight, so please if you don't mind, let's keep all reactions for later when you get home and let's let the congressman speak," Schwartz said. articles.title: FIRST ON FOX: Dems' affordability crusade collides with eye-popping price tag for socialist immigration plans
articles.summary: The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimates each illegal immigrant costs taxpayers $166,716 over their lifetime in a bombshell report.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: A new White House economic report warns that immigration policies backed by the Democratic Socialists of America could cost American taxpayers hundreds of billions of dollars over the next decade, as the Trump administration sounds the alarm over the potential financial consequences of mass amnesty and expanded federal benefits. As President Donald Trump touts 16 consecutive months without illegal immigrant releases at the southern border, a Council of Economic Advisers report estimates that mass amnesty and expanded federal benefits under Democratic Socialists of America-backed immigration policies could cost taxpayers between $440 billion and $613 billion over the next decade. Socialist-aligned candidates have gained ground in 2026, winning key Democratic primaries and expanding their influence within the party. "President Trump … supercharged ICE to remove criminal illegal aliens from our communities, including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members and terrorists," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. 'SQUAD' DEMOCRAT FORMALLY INTRODUCES BILL TO ABOLISH ICE, BORDER PATROL AND DISMANTLE DHS "Meanwhile, radical Democrats want to go back to their extreme open border policies and grant amnesty to the illegal aliens they released into our communities. Not only will these radical policies make America less safe, but they will cost the American taxpayer billions of dollars." With the midterms approaching and Democrats campaigning heavily on affordability, the White House is casting the DSA's immigration agenda as a potential financial and public safety threat — warning that its policies could compound the very cost-of-living pressures Democrats have used to hammer Republicans. DEMOCRATS SAY THEY'LL MAKE LIFE AFFORDABLE. YOUR WALLET MAY DISAGREE The council's findings go beyond the cost of mass amnesty, examining the potential impact of expanded federal benefits and reduced immigration enforcement, policies the White House warns could impose a significant financial burden on American families. The council estimates that the average illegal immigrant carries a lifetime net fiscal cost of $166,716, with the current illegal immigrant population projected to account for between $1.4 trillion and $1.9 trillion in taxpayer costs under its model — figures the administration is highlighting as the "true costs of extreme open borders [and] mass-amnesty socialist policies." CALIFORNIA FACES UNLIKELY TAX REVOLT AMID BILLIONS IN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT HEALTHCARE COSTS The CEA's estimated $166,716 lifetime taxpayer cost per illegal immigrant exceeds the roughly $124,000 it would cost to put a student through four years at an average in-state public university, including tuition, housing, food and other expenses, according to College Board's 2025–26 figures — putting the figure in perspective as American families also grapple with college affordability. The Council added that while illegal immigrants are generally prohibited from federal benefit programs, some on the left want to reverse that standard and provide subsidized healthcare and programs like food stamps to those in the country unlawfully. SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' Beyond expanded federal benefits, the council estimates that ending Trump-backed immigration enforcement measures would wipe out between $227 billion and $287 billion in projected taxpayer savings, producing a net estimated cost of $79 billion to $139 billion over the next decade after accounting for reduced enforcement spending. An interactive White House webpage released alongside the report allows Americans to explore the projected costs of "socialism" across several policy areas, with the council estimating that the Democratic Socialists of America's broader agenda could cost $49 trillion over ten years — roughly $355,000 per American household. That sweeping projection extends far beyond immigration, which the council separately estimates could cost between $440 billion and $613 billion over the next decade. DOJ THREATENS TO CUT BILLIONS IN WELFARE FUNDING FROM STATES FOR FAILING TO REPORT ILLEGAL MIGRANTS If the immigration policies examined in the report were implemented, the White House estimates that expanded eligibility for SNAP, federal housing assistance and Medicaid would add between $361 billion and $475 billion in federal spending over the next decade. The report estimated that expanding federal benefits under the proposed immigration policies would add $3.6 billion to $4.7 billion in annual food stamp costs, another $2.3 billion to $3 billion in federal housing assistance, and as much as $40 billion a year in additional Medicaid spending. US STATE DEPARTMENT HAS YANKED MORE THAN 175K VISAS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SO FAR Along with the report, the White House highlighted a 73% uptick in drug interdictions through August 2026 compared with the same period in fiscal year 2024, while separately pointing to declining fentanyl-related deaths as evidence of its broader border enforcement strategy. The administration also highlighted another key aspect of the immigration-cost paradigm that it changed — remarking that Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for certain foreign-national groups "returned … to its original purpose: temporary." TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SLASHES TIME REFUGEES HAVE TO CHALLENGE LOSS OF LEGAL STATUS The administration's efforts to terminate TPS designations for certain countries have faced legal challenges, underscoring the ongoing dispute over the scope of federal immigration authority. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The administration has also moved to end certain Temporary Protected Status designations and revoke more than 250,000 visas as part of its broader immigration crackdown, measures the White House has highlighted alongside its efforts to tighten enforcement and reduce what it says are substantial taxpayer costs.
