articles.title: ‘Big Condiment’ warning gets Warren roasted online over progressive's economic priorities
articles.summary: Elizabeth Warren's warning about the $45 billion McCormick-Unilever merger sparked online mockery, with users joking about "Big Condiment" prices.
articles.body: A post made by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., this week quickly became a punchline online after she warned that a proposed $45 billion deal bringing some of America’s best-known condiment and food brands under one roof could drive up grocery prices even further. The merger would combine McCormick brands such as Cholula and Frank’s RedHot with Unilever Foods products including Hellmann’s and Knorr. Warren argues the deal could weaken competition and leave shoppers with fewer choices. Users online joked about Warren cautioning against "Big Condiment." DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT "One company could soon control them all," Warren said of four popular condiments. "I have concerns that McCormick and Unilever's $45 billion merger could increase YOUR grocery prices." The post drew jokes from users who argued that housing, infrastructure and the national debt are bigger concerns than a potential rise in the prices of condiments. "Yes, a simultaneous increase in the prices of (checks notes) mayo and (checks notes again) hot sauce could bring the country to its knees," one user on X wrote. "The only thing raising my grocery prices is federal deficit and the resulting inflation you all seem to be ok with," another added. Venture capitalist Hank Medina sarcastically posted to his X account with 1.7 million followers, "The United States will crumble if big mayo merges with big hot sauce. SOUND THE ALARM FOLKS!!! We have no other condiment alternatives if this happens." But the real impact of a food merger is no laughing matter. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, accelerating from 3.4% in August, according to the latest Bureau of Labor Statistics report. Prices climbed 0.6% in September alone, underscoring the persistent affordability pressures facing American households just weeks before the midterm elections. Narrowing in on grocery prices, they rose 1.8% from a year ago but dipped 0.1% in September, while overall food prices were up 2.5% annually. With an affordability crisis plaguing the U.S. heading into the midterms, any threat of further impacts on Americans' pocketbooks is worth noting ahead of Election Day. Meanwhile, Warren has launched a broader campaign to challenge food-industry consolidation — not just against the recent condiment merger proposal. ECONOMIST CALLS OUT AMERICA’S SOCIALIST ELITE, SAYS THEY GOT RICH BASHING CAPITALISM In an Oct. 6 letter to the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission, she urged regulators to scrutinize the McCormick–Unilever deal alongside two other proposed food-industry mergers. The Massachusetts progressive argued the multibillion-dollar deal could reduce competition for shoppers' grocery dollars and retailers’ shelf space across overlapping pantry staples, leaving consumers with fewer choices and higher prices. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP If the deal announced in March were approved, it would combine McCormick with Unilever’s foods business in a transaction valued at about $45 billion. The combined company would bring together brands such as Cholula, Frank’s RedHot, Hellmann’s and Knorr. It is expected to close by mid-2027, subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals.

articles.title: Katie Zacharia did not pass the bar exam, senior administration official says
articles.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam when she took it after graduating from law school, according to a senior administration official.
articles.body: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia did not pass the California bar exam when she took it after graduating from law school, according to a senior administration official. The official argued that Zacharia could technically be considered a “lawyer,” though not an attorney. President Donald Trump referred to Zacharia as an “attorney” in his Truth Social post announcing that he was tapping her as press secretary. But several lawyers told NBC News that “lawyer” is widely understood to refer to someone who has passed the bar exam and is licensed to practice law. Zacharia’s failure to pass the bar exam was first reported by The Wall Street Journal. The new White House press secretary is facing questions about her legal credentials after the White House has not said whether Zacharia, who has repeatedly referred to herself as a lawyer, passed the bar exam. NBC News has not found evidence that she is licensed to practice law in any state. Zacharia, who graduated from Pepperdine Law, has said that she practiced law in China. Legal experts told NBC News that only Chinese citizens can sit for the Chinese bar exam. One expert told NBC News that Zacharia could have consulted on cross-border legal issues. The State Bar of California and the D.C. Bar didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on whether Zacharia could be considered a “lawyer.” Zacharia lived in California but said she would move to Washington, D.C., for her new job. The New York Times previously reported that Zacharia said in an interview that before she began appearing in cable news interviews, she discussed with Pepperdine’s president how to identify herself. Zacharia told The New York Times that she was told it was OK to use “lawyer,” but not “attorney” or “esquire.” Pepperdine didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. On Wednesday, representatives from the Democracy Defenders Fund, which frequently opposes the Trump administration, asked California Attorney General Rob Bonta and George Cardona, the chief trial attorney at the State Bar of California, to investigate whether Zacharia “engaged in the unauthorized practice of law.” Cardona’s office investigates potential lawyer misconduct. “Falsely holding oneself out as a lawyer is a criminal offense, punishable by fine or incarceration of up to a year in jail,” the letter said. The signatories of the letter included Norm Eisen, co-founder of the Democracy Defenders Fund, as well as Richard Painter, who served as President George W. Bush’s ethics lawyer. Painter, now a law professor at the University of Minnesota, has been a critic of Trump. Painter does not work at the Democracy Defenders Fund. The California Attorney General’s Office didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the letter. A spokesperson for the State Bar of California told NBC News that the bar “cannot confirm whether it has received any complaint or is conducting any investigation,” citing confidentiality requirements. Reached for comment, the White House referred to a post from White House communications director Steven Cheung, who criticized a different group that asked the State Bar of California to investigate Zacharia. In that post, Cheung referred to the watchdog group Campaign for Accountability as “a radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome.” Cheung also said in a statement that Zacharia “is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team.” “She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary,” he said. The White House also referred to a prior statement from Zacharia in which she said she “practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials.” A spokesperson for the State Bar of California previously told NBC News that the state does not have records of Zacharia having been licensed to practice law in the state. The spokesperson said that she never “appeared on a California bar exam pass list,” but declined to say whether she had ever sat for the bar exam, citing confidentiality requirements.

articles.title: Rep. Andy Harris threatens prosecution of student reporter for trying to record him after debate
articles.summary: A video taken by News4’s partners at The Baltimore Banner shows Rep.
articles.body: A video taken by News4’s partners at The Baltimore Banner shows Rep. Andy Harris, R-Md., telling a student reporter from the University of Maryland that she did not have permission to record him and threatening prosecution. “You do not have my permission to record! If you record, we will refer you to the prosecutor,” Harris told the student reporter. “Everyone in here is recording,” the student reporter said. “But you are not allowed to. We are in a two-party state,” Harris said, citing Maryland’s Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Act, which makes it a felony to record private conversations without consent from both participants. However, the law only protects private conversations, and recording is allowable in situations where there is no “reasonable expectation of privacy.” The exchange went on for several minutes. The reporter then tried to ask Harris his thoughts on the Iran war. “You said that it could’ve gone smoother and it could’ve gone better. What did you mean by that?” she asked. “You’re gonna have to take her camera,” said Harris, who is seeking re-election. “She is violating the law. In fact, get an officer in here.” News4 reached out to Harris’ office for comment but has not heard back. Harris, who is seeking a ninth term in the House, had just left a contentious debate, where he faced scrutiny from audience members over the Iran war and rising diesel prices. Banner reporter Pamela Wood shared in a social media post Wednesday that Harris invited reporters to interview him after the debate. The video shows several journalists participating in the postdebate gaggle. Attorney Kevin Goldberg, vice president of the Freedom Forum, a nonprofit that supports the First Amendment, said Maryland’s two-party consent laws wouldn’t apply in this case because Harris was speaking to a group of reporters in a public space. “If a reporter has a right to be in a space and work as a reporter, they cannot be denied that right simply because somebody doesn’t like the coverage or somebody doesn’t like the questions or somebody doesn’t like their viewpoint,” Goldberg said. This was how Harris’ conversation with the reporters eventually ended: “Congressman, you said that you supported the First Amendment — what does this say about that?” the college reporter asked. “All right guys, she’s ruining your chance to get an answer about anything. See y’all. Thank her profusely,” Harris replied. Harris’ Democratic opponent, Dan Schwartz, released a statement saying in part that the “message of the night was clear, Andy Harris is out of touch, out of practice talking to voters, and much more interested in picking fights and spinning his story than offering real answers.”

articles.title: 'Suspicious' mail with DSA-linked return address triggers FBI, Capitol Hill investigation
articles.summary: Senior Capitol Hill staff were warned about suspicious letters containing unknown substances mailed to multiple congressional offices nationwide.
articles.body: Senior Capitol Hill staff were warned that "multiple letters containing suspicious substances" were mailed out across the country and to multiple congressional offices on Thursday. An email notice obtained by Fox News Digital sent to chiefs of staff, administrative managers and state directors said the U.S. Postal Inspection Service, the FBI and U.S. Capitol Police were "investigating multiple letters containing suspicious substances that were mailed to various addresses nationwide, including multiple Congressional offices." "Law enforcement officials are working to intercept any additional letters before they are delivered, however, it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations," the notice from the U.S. Senate Sergeant at Arms read. ARMED MAN ARRESTED AT US CAPITOL BARRICADE AS POLICE PROBE WHY HE DROVE ONTO RESTRICTED GROUNDS The notice was first reported by Punchbowl News. An FBI spokesperson declined to confirm specific instances or letters, but said in a statement that, "The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices." "Some of the letters contained an unknown substance, and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident," the spokesperson said. "We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters. This FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens." DEPROGRAMMED: FORMER DSA INSIDER REVEALS ‘FRIGHTENING’ SOCIALIST AGENDA DROVE HIM FROM ‘EXTREME’ IDEOLOGY Included in the Senate Sergeant at Arms' notice was an image of one of the envelopes that included a return address in the top-left corner for the Democratic Socialists of America’s (DSA) headquarters in New York City. It is unclear whether the DSA had any involvement in sending the letters. Fox News Digital reached out to the DSA for comment but has not heard back.A representative for the organization told the New York Post that the DSA "has not occupied this office address since 2013." MASSIVE TROVE OF REPUBLICAN VOTER AND DONOR INFO BREACHED IN BIDEN DOJ PROBE: SENATE CHAIRMAN "We are also no longer headquartered at 75 Maiden Lane," the rep said. The notice warned that "all suspicious letters, packages, or substances should be treated as potentially hazardous." Suspicious letters were also sent to state elections offices around the country. The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors said in a joint statement that, "Those who administer our elections should never fear for their safety while carrying out their essential duties." "Election officials take these matters seriously and work closely with law enforcement and security partners to protect their personnel and facilities," the organizations said. "We have security measures and contingency plans in place to respond to potential threats and emergencies while maintaining essential election operations." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It comes on the 25-year anniversary after an anthrax-laced letter was opened by a staffer in then-Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle’s office on Oct. 15, 2001. Since then, Congress has drastically overhauled how it accepts mail. Packages and mail no longer come directly to the Hill, and instead are processed in facilities where they are screened and irradiated before making their way to a congressional office.

articles.title: Somalis in Minnesota unleash fury on Trump after feds raid Ilhan Omar's DC home
articles.summary: Minneapolis Somali community members say they feel personally attacked after federal agents raided Rep. Ilhan Omar's D.C. home in a citizenship probe.
articles.body: MINNEAPOLIS — Members of Minnesota's growing Somali community, including a city council member, tore into President Donald Trump and his administration when speaking with Fox News Digital after Monday's raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington, D.C., residence. "Somalis — we all feel attacked by President Trump," Jamal Osman, the Somali-born vice president of the Minneapolis City Council, said of the impact of the raid carried out by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents. "Our president has broken the law many times. ICE [is] terrorizing our community ... and we're not surprised such action has taken place," Osman continued in reference to the search of Omar's home. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION "We have seen the threats, the horrific language he uses against my community. It's unacceptable, and we're hoping this could stop," Osman said. A 37-year-old social worker and Minneapolis resident named Abdi, who declined to give his last name or be interviewed on camera, had even harsher words for the president. He, like Osman, said he was born in Somalia. "I feel like raiding a congresswoman — it feels like Donald Trump and his regime wanted to use their power to dehumanize and also humiliate someone that is part of the Congress," Abdi said. He claimed that Trump "hates Somali people because of Ilhan Omar." Abdi said Trump created "hate" and a "fight" with Somalis in America and claimed that they are being followed and harassed in the streets because of the president. TRUMP RALLY CROWD CHANTS 'DEPORT' AS PRESIDENT RIPS ILHAN OMAR AFTER FEDERAL RAID "It's personal," he said. "And Ilhan Omar — he doesn't treat her as a congressmember — he treats her as someone who's below him." "If they take the citizenship away from her, then I will say, ‘Are we in a dictatorship?’ That's using power to use against an American citizen, then maybe the thinking we have for the United States is completely different." Osman said the raid is proof of what the Trump administration is willing to do. "We live in the United States, which is the land of the laws. I don't expect Trump or anyone in this matter to break the U.S. Constitution," he continued. "There's laws. He can, of course, threaten, but there's a court process, there's due process. He can't say he's gonna deport her, he's gonna deport me, thousands of Somalis." OMAR RAID OUTRAGE GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE WHEN INTERNET NOTICES HER PAST 6-WORD CLAIM: 'COULDN'T AGREE MORE' Osman's message to the president was simple: "Stop it." "We're American citizens like everyone else," he said. A third person, a 22-year-old Somali American woman who declined to be named or filmed, told Fox News Digital that she wasn't surprised about the raid on Omar's home. "I thought it was bound to happen soon enough," she said. "They've been talking about her in a negative manner. The government [has been] constantly questioning her immigration status and her naturalization in the country. So it was bound to happen for them to investigate her soon enough." When reached about the comments from the Minneapolis Somali community, the White House pointed Fox News Digital to the president's public reaction to the raid on Monday. "I’ve always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me," Trump brushed off. "I think she’s a terrible person. Just a complainer. She comes from a country that is a non-country, and then she comes over here, and she complains about our Constitution." "I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ. I have nothing to do with it." ILHAN OMAR’S HUSBAND INSISTS HE HAS ‘NO CONCERNS’ AMID FEDERAL IMMIGRATION INVESTIGATION HSI, the principal investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), executed a search warrant at Omar's home in the nation's capital early Monday morning, as first reported by Fox News Digital. Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that the raid stems from an investigation into whether Omar or her late father, Nur Mohamed, fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork decades ago. The investigation, the sources note, could lead to the congresswoman's denaturalization. The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that Omar's phone, passport and computers were seized in the raid — it is not clear which other items or materials were taken from her residence, if any. Omar has not been seen since the raid, but offered her reaction to the unfolding investigation on social media Monday afternoon. "This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies. For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."

articles.title: Plenário do Senado discute PEC da Segurança Pública; votação pode ser ainda hoje
articles.summary: Tema é considerado prioritário para governo Lula, que pretende, após aprovação, criar o Ministério da Segurança Pública.
articles.body:
Tema é considerado prioritário para governo Lula, que pretende, após aprovação, criar o Ministério da Segurança Pública.

O plenário do Senado Federal deve votar nesta quinta-feira (15) a proposta de emenda à Constituição (PEC) da Segurança Pública .

Para ser aprovada, uma PEC precisa contar com o apoio de 49 senadores.

Ontem, a Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) do Senado concluiu a votação da proposta .

De acordo com o texto, União, Estados e Distrito Federal poderão criar leis na área de segurança pública, incluindo forças-tarefa intergovernamentais.

A proposta estabelece na Constituição o Sistema Único de Segurança Pública (SUSP), cujo objetivo é integrar o combate ao crime organizado entre os entes.

De acordo com o texto, União, Estados e Distrito Federal poderão criar leis na área de segurança pública, incluindo forças-tarefa intergovernamentais, organização das polícias e guardas municipais e do sistema socioeducativo.

Entre as medidas estão a obrigatoriedade de prisão em estabelecimento penal de segurança máxima ou de natureza especial.

Também fica proibida ou restringida a progressão de regime, a concessão de liberdade provisória, com ou sem fiança, e de saída temporária.

A PEC também permite a expropriação de todo e qualquer bem, direito ou valor econômico envolvido com as atividades criminosas. As regras valem para organizações criminosas, paramilitares e de milícia privada.

criação de polícias municipais para o policiamento ostensivo e comunitário;

ampliação da atuação da Polícia Rodoviária Federal (PRF) para o policiamento de hidrovias e ferrovias, além de apoiar outras forças de segurança, quando requisitada pelo governador;

manter a Polícia Federal e PRF sob competência privativa da União, assim como as normas para atividades de inteligência.

O PL e os partidos de oposição ao governo Lula (PT) no Senado apresentaram uma emenda para incluir a redução da maioridade penal na PEC da Segurança Pública.

A emenda proposta pela oposição incluiria duas alterações na proposta, reduzindo a maioridade penal:

para 16 anos para a maior parte dos crimes; e

para 14 anos para crimes hediondos, tortura, tráfico de drogas, terrorismo, organização criminosa, associação criminosa e outros.

Olá, boa tarde. Acompanhe a partir de agora a transmissão de sessão no Senado que vai debater a PEC da segurança pública.

articles.title: Bill and Hillary Clinton make eleventh-hour midterm moves as party's old guard faces new reality
articles.summary: Bill Clinton heads to Florida to campaign for David Jolly while Hillary Clinton launches "High Stakes" podcast with Kara Swisher for midterms.
articles.body: The Clintons are back on the midterm campaign circuit — with Bill Clinton heading to Florida to stump for Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Jolly and Hillary Clinton taking to the podcast microphone as the party makes its final push toward Election Day. The former president is scheduled to make his first public campaign appearance of the 2026 election cycle on Oct. 20 for Jolly, a former Republican congressman turned Democrat. Hillary, meanwhile, has teamed up with journalist Kara Swisher for a new midterm-focused podcast series and has been making campaign appearances of her own. The moves bring two of the Democratic Party's most recognizable figures into the midterm fight as the party grapples with competing visions for its future, raising questions about how much influence the Clintons still wield as progressive candidates challenge the Democratic establishment. BIDEN CONSPICUOUSLY ABSENT FROM CAMPAIGN TRAIL AS OBAMA, HARRIS STEP UP FOR MIDTERM PUSH While the Clintons remain prominent in Democratic politics, one party strategist says Democrats are more focused on winning elections than revisiting the party's past. "President Clinton remains one of the most gifted political communicators this country has ever known, particularly when it comes to connecting with working-class voters on the economic issues that matter most," said Democratic strategist Kevin Walling. "But I don’t believe that Democrats are looking for a Clinton restoration — they’re looking for a path back to winning." Democratic strategist Mally Smith offered a more skeptical assessment of how much reach the Clintons have in the closing weeks of the election. "Hillary and Bill are still relevant to some voters. However, they will mostly be useful in speaking to the Democratic base and those who are highly engaged in politics," said Smith. "It is a hard media environment to breakthrough and even current elected officials, let alone former office holders, will struggle to get people’s attention." Clinton's Oct. 20 appearance will take place at an interfaith event in Hollywood, Florida, alongside Jolly, who is facing Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in the race to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. Jolly is campaigning on affordability, including lowering property insurance costs through a state-backed catastrophe fund, expanding Medicaid, increasing funding for public schools and protecting abortion rights. Hillary Clinton, meanwhile, traveled to Omaha, Nebraska, on Saturday to rally support for Democratic candidates Lynne Walz and Denise Powell at a "Pumpkins, Pies, and Politics" fundraiser. HILLARY CLINTON ISSUES ENDORSEMENT IN US MIDTERM ELECTIONS Asked how she would address Democrats who feel their votes no longer matter, Clinton pointed to a series of national crises that have contributed to voter frustration — including her 2016 election loss. "And you could kind of understand that, for people who feel like they've had a series of hard times. If you look back on the last 25 years in our country, I was a senator from New York on 9/11. That was a trauma. The terrible financial crisis of 2008 was horrific for people. We had an election in 2016 that, you know, raised a lot of questions that we're still trying to find answers for about what, what kind of really went on, and then we had COVID," she said during the Nebraska event. Clinton teamed up with journalist and podcast host Kara Swisher for a six-week limited series titled "High Stakes," which debuted Oct. 14 and will air weekly through mid-November, focusing on the 2026 midterm elections, key congressional races and issues. The first episode, which aired Wednesday, centered on rising costs for gas, groceries and healthcare, Elon Musk's political spending and how Democrats can make affordability a winning message, while also examining key Senate races in Michigan and Maine. HILLARY CLINTON CONCEDES INFAMOUS 9/11 NEAR-FAINTING EPISODE IN 2016 WAS A 'MISTAKE' ON HER PART "If the former president can help Democrats compete in a challenging state like Florida, and Secretary Clinton’s podcast can contribute to a substantive national conversation that motivates my party, that’s certainly a positive," said Walling. The Clintons' increased visibility comes as Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates have scored primary victories against incumbent or establishment-backed Democrats in states including Colorado, New York and Michigan. MEET THE FAR-LEFT INSURGENTS WAGING WAR ON THE DEMOCRATIC ESTABLISHMENT IN 2026 MIDTERMS "The challenge for Democrats is drawing on the wisdom and experience of the party’s past without overshadowing the next generation of leaders who will define its future," he added. articles.title: Federal authorities investigate suspicious mailings sent to congressional and secretary of state offices
articles.summary: The FBI, U.S. Capitol Police and U.S.
articles.body: The FBI, U.S. Capitol Police and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating letters containing suspicious substances that were mailed to “various addresses nationwide, including multiple Congressional offices,” according to a notice that senior staff in Senate offices received Thursday morning. “Law enforcement officials are working to intercept any additional letters before they are delivered, however, it is possible that some letters may reach their destinations,” the notice said, according to two people who received it. The notice included an image of one of the suspicious envelopes and said that the letters “may contain different variations of postage stamps.” It also warned that suspicious letters, packages or substances “should be treated as potentially hazardous and handled in accordance with established safety protocols.” The notice outlined how staff should handle the items and noted that mail and packages delivered to Senate offices or the Capitol complex are screened and tested for potential threats. A similar notice was sent to House lawmakers and staff Thursday from the House sergeant at arms. The notice said that while mail and packages delivered to the House offices in the Capitol are rigorously screened, district offices should be use safe mail handling procedures, including the use of “mail hoods” — screening equipment that allows the handling of mail without exposing staff to danger — provided by the sergeant at arms, according to two congressional offices who shared the message with NBC News. The U.S. Postal Inspection Service and Capitol Police referred questions from NBC News to the FBI, which confirmed in a statement that the agencies are investigating “a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices.” The agency did not specify the locations of the offices targeted. “Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident,” the statement said. “We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters.” The notice sent to Senate staff did not say whether the congressional offices involved are the ones in Washington, D.C. or local and regional offices. Congress is on recess leading up to the midterm elections, so most lawmakers are back home in their districts as they campaign in the final weeks of the races. Congressional staff, however, are still on the Capitol campus. An office for Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., was among those targeted, a spokesperson for the senator told NBC News in a statement. “We received the notification from the FBI that one of our offices was mailed a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted by USPS. Follow up questions should be directed to the FBI.” A letter with a suspicious substance was also sent to Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy’s Hartford, Connecticut, office, his spokesperson, Josh Sorbe, said in a statement. The FBI, Capitol Police and sergeant at arms informed the office about the letter, Sorbe said, adding that the senator and his staff “were not in immediate danger.” NBC News reported Wednesday that secretaries of state’s offices in Louisiana, Ohio and Oklahoma were sent packages this week containing mysterious powders. Oklahoma and Louisiana reported receiving the envelopes, while Ohio said U.S. Postal Service investigators intercepted a package destined for it. These offices oversee and manage the election process in their respective states, and these incidents come just weeks before Election Day on Nov. 3.

articles.title: Kumaraswamy calls Shivakumar ‘Sting Samrat’, seeks probe by sitting high court judge
articles.summary: HD Kumaraswamy calls Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar “Sting Samrat,” seeks sitting HC judge probe into alleged stings targeting Siddaramaiah and others.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Union minister HD Kumaraswamy Thursday called chief minister DK Shivakumar “Sting Samrat” and demanded an inquiry by a sitting high court judge into alleged clandestine operations targeting former CM Siddaramaiah and others.Suggesting Shivakumar was at the heart of alleged sting operations, Kumaraswamy wanted investigators to examine Shivakumar’s phone records to establish facts and unearth the truth. His allegations could not be independently verified. The probe, he said, should be free of political interference.He also sought an investigation into the role of Rakesh Shetty, MD of a private Kannada channel, and Krupa Alva, former chairperson of Karnataka State Commission for Protection of Child Rights, suspecting their role in the operation linked to Siddaramaiah.Kumaraswamy alleged Shivakumar had a lengthy meeting at a five-star hotel in Bengaluru recently with a person allegedly involved in sting operations, and later warned five of his cabinet colleagues that they had been targeted.He recalled a 2024 remark by BJP MLA and former minister Ramesh Jarkiholi — who was forced to resign after a video purportedly showing him in a compromising position emerged — that indirectly targeted Shivakumar and had suggested videos involving other political figures, including Siddaramaiah and deputy CM G Parameshwara, could emerge. “That is why I called him ‘Sting Samarat’. The CM’s mindset is a matter of concern,” he said.Dismissing the charge that he envied Shivakumar for becoming CM, Kumaraswamy said he had “already held the post, enjoyed it and was not seeking it again”. He accused Congress functionaries of abusing him daily to please Shivakumar. “If you think criticising me will make the CM happy, you can abuse me even more,” he said.He hit back at home minister Priyank Kharge, saying: “I can fall asleep within two minutes after finishing my work. You can’t because you are worried about the I-T department and the Enforcement Directorate. I have nothing to worry about.”Taking a swipe at Kumaraswamy, Priyank had said: “I did not fear your father RSS, so why should I fear you?”Also Thursday, Kumaraswamy staged a dharna outside Bengaluru city police commissioner’s office Thursday, demanding a probe into the alleged sting operation targeting Siddaramaiah. Accompanied by JD(S) members, Kumaraswamy also met police commissioner Seemanth Kumar Singh for about 30 minutes. “Based on the assurance given by the police commissioner, I’ll give the govt two days to act,” he said. Responding to Priyank comment that he could also be interrogated, Kumaraswamy said, “I am here. Let police question me.”In Mangaluru, Shivakumar declined to comment on allegations linking him to the alleged sting operation targeting Siddaramaiah, saying he had “no information” on the issue. However, Dakshina Kannada district minister UT Khader said an investigation is under way and it would establish facts. “They (opposition) were the ones who demanded an inquiry, so why are they sitting on dharna and protesting?” Khader said. “Let the investigation proceed. articles.title: Trump-appointed justice joins Sotomayor in unlikely alliance to rip DOJ's handling of illegal immigrant case
articles.summary: Supreme Court Justices Neil Gorsuch and Sonia Sotomayor joined forces after prosecutors charged a deported man despite ordering him to stay in Oklahoma after his first conviction.
articles.body: Conservative Supreme Court Justice Neil Gorsuch has joined forces with liberal Justice Sonia Sotomayor to question the federal government's prosecution of an illegal immigrant, marking the latest unlikely alliance between the two justices. Gorsuch, appointed by President Donald Trump, and Sotomayor, appointed by former President Barack Obama, raised concerns about the government's decision to prosecute a Mexican national twice for being found unlawfully in the United States — even after a federal court prohibited him from leaving the Eastern District of Oklahoma following his first conviction. The unlikely pairing emerged Tuesday when the Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal from Jesus Herrera-Salazar, who argued that his second prosecution violated the Fifth Amendment's protection against double jeopardy. Although the justices agreed the Court should not take up the case, Sotomayor issued a separate statement, joined by Gorsuch, warning of serious constitutional problems with the government's actions. GORSUCH SAYS IDEOLOGICAL DIVIDES ON SUPREME COURT COME DOWN TO ‘HOW YOU READ LAW,’ NOT POLITICS "From the moment he was released from custody after serving his first term of imprisonment, Herrera-Salazar was presented with a Hobson's choice," Sotomayor wrote in the statement joined by Gorsuch. "In the Government's eyes, whether Herrera-Salazar remained in the Eastern District of Oklahoma or left the United States, he would be breaking the law." The two justices questioned how the government could punish someone for remaining in the country after effectively prohibiting him from leaving, with the pair's joint statement describing the situation as a "constitutional absurdity." Their agreement is particularly noteworthy given their differing judicial philosophies, but it is not the first time the pair has found common ground over constitutional protections against government action. In November 2024, Sotomayor and Gorsuch jointly questioned whether homeowners should be compensated when police destroy private property while carrying out law enforcement operations. A few months later, they again joined forces to raise concerns about warrantless misdemeanor arrests. In both cases, as in the latest immigration dispute, the Court declined to hear the appeals, but the justices issued statements highlighting constitutional questions they believed deserved attention. The pair's latest expression of joint public concern came after Herrera-Salazar, a Mexican national previously removed from the United States, was indicted in 2020 for being found in the country following deportation, a violation of federal immigration law. 'UNPRECEDENTED': JUDGES REVEAL BEHIND-THE-SCENES COORDINATION ON TRUMP IMMIGRATION CASES He pleaded guilty and served a prison sentence before being placed on supervised release, during which he was expressly prohibited from leaving the Eastern District of Oklahoma without authorization under the terms of his release. While still under those restrictions, Herrera-Salazar was stopped by police in Heavener, Oklahoma, and subsequently charged again under the same federal immigration statute prohibiting previously deported individuals from being found unlawfully in the United States. A jury subsequently convicted Herrera-Salazar, resulting in another prison sentence and additional supervised release. The second prosecution prompted Herrera-Salazar to challenge his conviction on double-jeopardy grounds, arguing that the government had effectively punished him twice for the same continuous period of unlawful presence. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected that argument, concluding that the offense is completed when authorities discover a person's unlawful presence and that a subsequent discovery can support a separate prosecution without requiring another illegal entry. Sotomayor and Gorsuch questioned that reasoning, pointing to Supreme Court precedent establishing that prosecutors cannot evade double-jeopardy protections simply by dividing one continuous crime into separate periods. Their concern was not whether Herrera-Salazar had violated immigration law in the first place, but whether the government could repeatedly prosecute him for remaining in the United States without evidence of a separate unlawful reentry. The justices also highlighted that Herrera-Salazar's supervised-release conditions restricted him from leaving Oklahoma, meaning the government was effectively preventing him from ending the conduct for which it later prosecuted him again. Sotomayor warned that, under the government's interpretation, prosecutors theoretically could have brought separate charges against Herrera-Salazar for each day he remained imprisoned following his first conviction. The statement was issued despite the justices' agreement with the Court's decision not to review the case. Sotomayor explained that Herrera-Salazar had already been removed from the United States and expressed hope that the unusual circumstances surrounding his prosecution would not arise again. SUPREME COURT KICKS OFF NEW TERM WITH FRESH QUESTIONS OVER ITS LEGITIMACY AND ITS FUTURE Rather than dissenting from the Court's refusal to hear the appeal, Sotomayor and Gorsuch used what is formally known as a statement "respecting the denial of certiorari" to publicly identify constitutional concerns and urge lower courts to avoid similar problems in future cases. The unusual collaboration follows two earlier cases in which Sotomayor authored statements joined by Gorsuch after the Supreme Court declined review. In November 2024, the pair raised concerns in Baker v. City of McKinney, a Texas case involving a homeowner whose property was extensively damaged during a police operation to apprehend an armed fugitive. Police had used tear gas, explosives and an armored vehicle during the standoff, leaving the home severely damaged. Although the justices acknowledged that officers acted properly to protect public safety, they questioned whether the Constitution permits the government to impose the financial burden of such damage on an individual homeowner without compensation. Meanwhile, in February 2025, Sotomayor and Gorsuch again joined forces, this time questioning whether the Fourth Amendment permitted police to make warrantless arrests for misdemeanors committed outside an officer's presence that they did not personally witness.
